records.name: Thomas Fairfax, 6th Lord Fairfax of Cameron
records.scaleNote: Proprietor of the c. 5.2-million-acre Northern Neck Proprietary; press reporting on the 2021 renaming of Lord Fairfax Community College stated he held at least 97 enslaved people at his death.
records.base: Greenway Court, White Post (now Clarke County), Virginia
records.origins: An English-born Scottish peer, he inherited the Northern Neck Proprietary through his mother, Catherine Culpeper, daughter of Governor Thomas Lord Culpeper. He moved to Virginia in 1747, first to his cousin William Fairfax's Belvoir plantation and then to Greenway Court in the Shenandoah Valley, the only British peer to live permanently in colonial America.
records.role_summary: Fairfax granted and rented out land across the Northern Neck (millions of acres between the Rappahannock and Potomac) and collected quitrents from planters whose wealth came from enslaved labour. He himself held enslaved people at Greenway Court and his other quarters, buying and selling them; he hired the teenage George Washington as a surveyor.

roleDetail.d: As proprietor he issued grants such as the 50,212 acres to Robert 'King' Carter's family, land worked by enslaved people; his quitrent income rested on that system.

Reports on the community-college renaming in 2021 said he owned at least 97 enslaved people when he died in 1781; an NPS survey records their quarters as log huts scattered in the woods near the manor.
He employed George Washington as a surveyor in 1748, beginning the Fairfax–Washington ties that shaped northern Virginia's planter elite.

records.legacy: His proprietary was confiscated piecemeal after the Revolution and the land passed to Virginia grantees and to heirs who sold it. His name is on Fairfax County, the City of Fairfax and thousands of local institutions; in 2021 the Lord Fairfax Community College board voted to drop his name because he was an enslaver.

legacyDetail.d: Lord Fairfax Community College in Middletown became Laurel Ridge Community College (2022) after its board cited his slaveholding.
Fairfax County's seal still uses a version of his arms; in 2021 the county's history commission said reviewing it was not a priority.

Greenway Court's land office survives on private land; the 6th Lord, unmarried, left no direct descendants.

records.name: Thomas Culpeper, 2nd Baron Culpeper of Thoresway
records.scaleNote: Governor of Virginia 1677–83 (mostly absent) and proprietor of the Northern Neck; no documented enslaving of his own, but his tenure coincided with the shift from servants to enslaved Africans after Bacon's Rebellion.
records.origins: A royalist courtier, he succeeded his father as baron at the Restoration and was governor of the Isle of Wight. In 1673 he and Henry Bennet, Earl of Arlington, received a 31-year grant of Virginia's quitrents and escheats, and in 1675 a patent to succeed Sir William Berkeley as governor.
records.role_summary: No documented direct ownership of enslaved people. As governor (1677–83) he visited Virginia briefly in 1680 and 1682–83; the 1680 assembly session he presided over is generally dated as passing an act 'for preventing Negroes Insurrections', and he consolidated the Northern Neck Proprietary that the Fairfax family later inherited.

roleDetail.d: He bought out most other claimants by 1681; James II confirmed the proprietary in 1688 and it passed to the Fairfaxes after his daughter's death in 1719.
Historians date the rapid replacement of white servants by enslaved Africans in Virginia to the 1680s, the years of his governorship.
His 1673 joint grant with Arlington of Virginia's quitrents was resented in the colony and surrendered in part in 1684.

records.legacy: The barony became extinct in 1725. His proprietary created the Fairfax land empire of northern Virginia, and Culpeper County (1749) and the town of Culpeper bear the family name.

legacyDetail.d: The Library of Virginia says Culpeper County was probably named for Catherine Culpeper, her mother Margaret, Thomas Lord Culpeper, or the family generally.

lineage.name: John Culpeper, 1st Baron Culpeper
lineage.note: Royalist granted the Northern Neck by the exiled Charles II in 1649.

lineage.name: Katherine Culpeper, Lady Fairfax
lineage.note: Married Thomas, 5th Lord Fairfax; her son inherited the proprietary.

lineage.name: Thomas, 6th Lord Fairfax
lineage.note: Took up residence in Virginia and ran the proprietary.

records.today: The Culpeper barony became extinct in 1725. His proprietary rights flowed to the Fairfax family; no publicly documented direct descendants of his are associated with the Virginia link beyond the Fairfax title.

records.name: Henry Bennet, 1st Earl of Arlington
records.scaleNote: Listed as a member/subscriber in the Royal African Company's 1672 charter; co-grantee of Virginia's quitrents in 1673.
records.origins: Secretary of State to Charles II and a member of the 'Cabal' ministry, he was created Earl of Arlington in April 1672.
records.role_summary: Arlington was one of the courtiers who subscribed to the Royal African Company when it was rechartered in September 1672, the company that shipped more enslaved Africans than any other British institution in the late 17th century. With Lord Culpeper he received a 1673 grant of Virginia's quitrents and escheats.

roleDetail.d: The charter's list of members names 'Henry, Earl of Arlington' alongside the Duke of York, Prince Rupert and Shaftesbury.
The 1673 Arlington–Culpeper grant of quitrents provoked Virginian protest and was surrendered in part in 1684.

records.legacy: Arlington County, Virginia, is only indirectly linked to him. The county (renamed from Alexandria County in 1920) took its name from G. W. P. Custis's Arlington House, which took the name of the Custis family's Eastern Shore estate; local historians dispute whether that estate was named for the earl or for Arlington, Gloucestershire.

legacyDetail.d: Arlington Magazine and the Arlington Historical Society note the Custis estate may predate his 1672 title, so the earl is at most a possible indirect namesake.

lineage.name: Isabella Bennet, Duchess of Grafton
lineage.note: Married Henry FitzRoy, 1st Duke of Grafton (son of Charles II); the Arlington titles passed through her.

records.today: His earldom passed via his daughter to the Dukes of Grafton (FitzRoy family); the Arlington link to slavery was not inherited as an enterprise. No publicly documented descendants have addressed the link.
placesNamed: Arlington County, Virginia (indirect and contested, via the Custis 'Arlington' estates)

records.name: Sir William Berkeley
records.scaleNote: Governor 1641–52 and 1660–77, when Virginia enacted the 1662 hereditary-slavery law and the 1667 and 1669 acts; held servants and enslaved workers at Green Spring.
records.base: Green Spring plantation, James City County, Virginia
records.origins: A courtier and playwright from a Somerset gentry family, Charles I named him governor of Virginia in 1641. He built Green Spring near Jamestown, experimenting with crops, and returned to power at the Restoration in 1660.
records.role_summary: Berkeley presided over the assembly sessions that turned slavery into a hereditary, racial legal status: the 1662 act making a child's status follow the mother, the 1667 act that baptism did not free, and the 1669 act exempting masters who killed enslaved people during 'correction'. He was also one of the eight Lords Proprietors of Carolina (1663).

roleDetail.d: The 1662 partus act, the 1667 baptism act and the 1669 'casual killing' act were all passed by assemblies he governed (Encyclopedia Virginia primary documents).
NPS records that he worked Green Spring with servants and enslaved labour; one account credits enslaved Africans with advising rice cultivation there.
His 1676–77 suppression of Bacon's Rebellion is widely seen as hastening planters' turn from indentured servants to enslaved Africans.

records.legacy: He died in London in 1677 after being recalled. Green Spring passed to his widow Frances Culpeper Berkeley and later to the Ludwell family; it is now part of Colonial National Historical Park (NPS).

legacyDetail.d: Green Spring's archaeological remains are managed by the National Park Service as part of Jamestown/Colonial NHP.

lineage.name: Frances Culpeper Stephens Berkeley
lineage.note: Married 1670; inherited Green Spring and later married Philip Ludwell.

lineage.name: Philip Ludwell
lineage.note: Frances's third husband; Green Spring stayed with the Ludwell–Lee line.

records.today: Berkeley left no children. Green Spring passed through the Ludwell family; no publicly documented descendants exist. The site is federal parkland.

records.name: Alexander Spotswood
records.scaleNote: Lieutenant governor 1710–22; held an 86,000-acre Spotsylvania grant and ran the South's first ironworks with enslaved labour (Encyclopedia Virginia gives no headcount).
records.origins: Born in the English garrison at Tangier, he was a career soldier wounded at Blenheim. Queen Anne commissioned him lieutenant governor of Virginia in 1710, deputising for the absentee Earl of Orkney.
records.role_summary: Spotswood used his office to secure 86,000 acres in the new county named for him, settled German miners at Germanna and built ironworks that Encyclopedia Virginia says 'relied on slave labor'. He became the largest iron producer in the colonies, exporting pig iron to England.

roleDetail.d: Encyclopedia Virginia: he built the South's first ironworks and, like tobacco planters, relied on enslaved labour to run them.
The Council granted him 86,000 acres in Spotsylvania in 1720, far above the Board of Trade's 1,000-acre limit, a factor in his 1722 removal.
He crossed the Blue Ridge in 1716 and ran the Virginia Indian Company monopoly (disallowed 1717); he also sent the expedition that killed Blackbeard in 1718.

records.legacy: His Germanna house was abandoned by c.1750; the site is studied by the Germanna Foundation and Mary Washington archaeologists. His grandson Alexander Spotswood corresponded with George Washington, who wrote to him in 1794 that he was 'principled against selling negroes'.

legacyDetail.d: Spotsylvania County (1720) and Germanna Community College recall him and his settlement.

lineage.name: Anne Butler Brayne Spotswood
lineage.note: Married in London; four children.

lineage.name: John Spotswood
lineage.note: Inherited the Spotsylvania lands and ironworks.

lineage.name: Alexander Spotswood
lineage.note: Revolutionary officer; married a niece of George Washington and received Washington's 1794 letter on not selling enslaved people.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants are associated with the slavery link today. The Germanna site and ironworks are archaeological sites; Spotsylvania County carries his name.

records.name: Hugh Drysdale
records.scaleNote: Lieutenant governor 1722–26 who proposed the 1723 slave-crimes act that restricted manumission and disfranchised free Black men.
records.origins: An Irish-born army officer, he was appointed lieutenant governor in April 1722 after the Crown removed Spotswood.
records.role_summary: Drysdale summoned the May 1723 assembly amid rumours of an enslaved people's conspiracy and proposed reforms to the laws on 'crimes committed by slaves'. The resulting act tightened trials of enslaved people, barred manumission except for 'meritorious services' approved by governor and council, and stripped free Black, mixed-race and Indian men of the vote.

roleDetail.d: Encyclopedia Virginia: he proposed reforms to militia laws and to the laws on crimes by enslaved people that 'helped calm fears following rumors of an insurrection'.
He signed a duty on imported alcohol and enslaved people, but British slave traders lobbied the Crown to disallow it.

records.legacy: He died in office in 1726 and was buried at Bruton Parish Church. The 1723 manumission restriction lasted until 1782.

legacyDetail.d: Private manumission in Virginia stayed effectively banned from 1723 until the 1782 manumission act.

lineage.name: Hester Drysdale
lineage.note: Lived with him at the Governor's Palace.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants have been traced. No county bears his name.

records.name: Sir William Gooch, 1st Baronet
records.scaleNote: Lieutenant governor 1727–49, the era of heavy slave imports; defended the 1723 disfranchisement of free Black men to the Board of Trade (1735/36).
records.origins: A soldier from Great Yarmouth, Norfolk, he served under Marlborough and was appointed lieutenant governor of Virginia in 1727.
records.role_summary: Gooch governed during the decades when imports of enslaved Africans into Virginia peaked and the planter class's investment in enslaved people grew. When the Board of Trade questioned the 1723 law denying free Black men the vote, Gooch defended it (1735/36), citing a recent conspiracy and saying free people of colour should be marked apart; the Crown accepted his explanation.

roleDetail.d: Encyclopedia Virginia reproduces his reply to Alured Popple of the Board of Trade justifying the 1723 law; the Crown let it stand.
A 1728 forty-shilling duty on each imported enslaved person was disallowed by the Crown; a later act shifted the tax to buyers.
His Tobacco Inspection Act strengthened the export economy built on enslaved labour.

records.legacy: He was made a baronet in 1746; the baronetcy passed to his brother Thomas Gooch, Bishop of Ely, and the Gooch baronets of Benacre, Suffolk, continue. Goochland County (1728) and Staunton (named for his wife Rebecca Staunton) recall him.

legacyDetail.d: Wikipedia notes the 7,000-acre Benacre Hall estate was separated from the baronetcy after the 13th baronet's death in 2008.

lineage.name: Rebecca Staunton, Lady Gooch
lineage.note: Staunton, Virginia, was named for her in 1749.

lineage.name: Sir Thomas Gooch, 2nd Baronet
lineage.note: Bishop of Ely; inherited the baronetcy because William's only son and grandson died before him.

records.today: The Gooch baronetcy (of Benacre) still exists in the brother's line; no living baronet has publicly addressed the Virginia link. Goochland County and the city of Staunton carry the family names.

records.name: Robert Dinwiddie
records.scaleNote: Lieutenant governor 1751–58 and earlier customs surveyor general whose district included Jamaica and the Carolinas; Encyclopedia Virginia records no enslaving by him.
records.origins: Born near Glasgow to a merchant family, he was a customs officer in Bermuda and from 1738 surveyor general of customs for the southern colonies, including Jamaica and the Bahamas.
records.role_summary: No documented personal enslaving in Encyclopedia Virginia's account. His relevance is as the Crown's customs officer for slave-economy colonies and as lieutenant governor of a slave society, who sent George Washington west in 1753 and helped start the French and Indian War.

roleDetail.d: As surveyor general (1738) he oversaw customs in Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia, the Carolinas, the Bahamas and Jamaica.
His administration rested on the militia and patrol system that policed enslaved Virginians, but his own role in it is not specifically documented.

records.legacy: He left Virginia in 1758 and died at Clifton, Bristol, leaving £10,000 to each of his two daughters. Dinwiddie County (1752) is named for him.

legacyDetail.d: The General Assembly named Dinwiddie County for him in his first session, 1752.

lineage.name: Rebecca Auchinleck (Affleck) Dinwiddie
lineage.note: Received a £350 annuity under his will.

lineage.name: John Dinwiddie
lineage.note: Emigrated to Virginia as a merchant.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants have been traced; his estate went to his two daughters.

records.name: Francis Fauquier
records.scaleNote: South Sea Company director 1748–57 (salary £150) and inheritor of £20,000 in South Sea stock; as lieutenant governor 1758–68 he held at least twelve adult enslaved people.
records.origins: Son of a Huguenot financier who was deputy master of the Mint under Newton and a Bank of England director, he inherited £20,000 in South Sea Company stock. He was a fellow of the Royal Society and a governor of the Foundling Hospital before being appointed to Virginia in 1758.
records.role_summary: Fauquier was a director of the South Sea Company, holder of the British asiento slave-trading contract, from 1748 to 1757. In Virginia he held enslaved people; his 1767 will lamented that his way of life there required it, let his twelve adult enslaved people choose new owners and forbade separating mothers from children — but did not free them.

roleDetail.d: Encyclopedia Virginia: director 1748–1757 at £150 a year; his father had left him £20,000 in its stock.
He let his twelve adult enslaved people pick their buyers and kept mothers and children together, while expressing regret at owning people.
He hosted Thomas Jefferson at Palace dinners in the 1760s.

records.legacy: He died at the Palace in 1768 and is buried at Bruton Parish Church. Fauquier County (1759) is named for him.

legacyDetail.d: His will is often quoted as an example of an enslaver's moral unease that stopped short of emancipation.

lineage.name: John Francis Fauquier
lineage.note: Huguenot financier, deputy master of the Mint and Bank of England director; left Francis £20,000 in South Sea stock and £5,000 in bank stock.

lineage.name: Catherine Dalston Fauquier
lineage.note: Mother of their two sons.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants have been traced. His family's wealth was in South Sea and Bank of England stock rather than land.

records.name: Norborne Berkeley, Baron de Botetourt
records.scaleNote: Royal governor 1768–70; his estate inventory lists at least eight enslaved people at the Governor's Palace (Colonial Williamsburg, DAACS).
records.origins: A Gloucestershire MP and courtier, he revived the barony of Botetourt in 1764 and was sent as resident governor of Virginia in 1768.
records.role_summary: Botetourt bought enslaved workers after arriving with white servants; Colonial Williamsburg names Hannah (who chose him as her enslaver after Fauquier's death), Cesar, Dan, Matt Piper, Doll, Phillis, Sally and her child Billy, and notes his household regularly flogged them after his first year.

roleDetail.d: His post-death inventory names the enslaved people in the Governor's Palace household.
Colonial Williamsburg reports household records of regular whipping of the enslaved workers.

records.legacy: Popular in Virginia, he died in office in 1770; the House of Burgesses commissioned a marble statue now at William & Mary, and Botetourt County and Berkeley County (now WV) were named for him.

legacyDetail.d: The Botetourt statue remains a campus landmark; William & Mary's 'Lemon Project' studies the college's ties to slavery.

lineage.name: Elizabeth Berkeley, Duchess of Beaufort
lineage.note: His barony was revived in 1803 for her son, the 5th Duke of Beaufort.

lineage.name: Dukes of Beaufort (Somerset family)
lineage.note: Held the Botetourt barony until the 10th Duke died in 1984; it is now in abeyance.

records.today: The barony of Botetourt has been in abeyance since 1984; it was held by the Somerset Dukes of Beaufort from 1803. He had no children.

records.name: John Murray, 4th Earl of Dunmore
records.scaleNote: Royal governor 1771–75; his Loyalist claim listed 57 enslaved people; his 1775 proclamation drew several hundred to 2,000 freedom-seekers (estimates vary) to British lines.
records.base: Governor's Palace, Williamsburg (and Porto Bello plantation, York County)
records.origins: A Scottish peer, governor of New York (1770–71) and then of Virginia. He bought Porto Bello plantation in York County and enslaved labourers there and at the Palace.
records.role_summary: On 7 November 1775 Dunmore offered freedom to enslaved people and servants of rebels who would fight for the King, forming the 'Ethiopian Regiment'. It was a military tactic: he did not free his own enslaved people, and he later governed the Bahamas (1787–96), a slave colony.

roleDetail.d: Encyclopedia Virginia: he purchased a York County plantation and enslaved labourers for it and the Palace; DAACS cites 57 people in his Loyalist claim.
Promised freedom to enslaved people of Patriots who joined British forces; hundreds formed Lord Dunmore's Ethiopian Regiment, many dying of smallpox.
Encyclopedia Virginia notes he kept his own enslaved labourers in bondage.

records.legacy: The proclamation pushed undecided planters to the Patriot side and became a precedent for wartime emancipation offers. Dunmore County (1772) was renamed Shenandoah County in 1778.

legacyDetail.d: Virginia erased his name in 1778, renaming Dunmore County as Shenandoah County.

lineage.name: Lady Charlotte Stewart, Countess of Dunmore
lineage.note: Their daughter born in 1774 was named Virginia.

records.name: John Campbell, 4th Earl of Loudoun
records.scaleNote: Titular governor-general of Virginia 1756–59 and British commander-in-chief in North America; no documented slaveholding or slave-trade investment found.
records.origins: A Scottish peer and soldier who fought the Jacobites in 1745, he was sent to North America in 1756 as commander-in-chief and governor-general of Virginia, a largely titular post exercised by Dinwiddie and Fauquier.
records.role_summary: No documented direct involvement in slavery; his tie is as the absentee Crown governor of a slave colony during the French and Indian War. He was recalled in 1757 after military failures and an unpopular embargo on colonial shipping.

roleDetail.d: His salary and title came from a colony whose revenues rested on tobacco grown by enslaved people; the work was done by lieutenant governors.
The Huntington Library holds c. 8,000 items of his papers (bulk 1755–58), a major source on the war.

records.legacy: Loudoun County (1757) is named for him. He died unmarried in 1782 and the earldom passed to a cousin and later through the female line.

legacyDetail.d: The Scottish earldom can pass through women; it is now held by the Abney-Hastings family.

records.name: William Anne Keppel, 2nd Earl of Albemarle
records.scaleNote: Absentee governor of Virginia 1737–54 who never visited; his sons George (3rd Earl) and Augustus Keppel led the 1762 capture of Havana and the 1758 capture of Gorée.
records.origins: Son of Arnold Joost van Keppel, the Dutch favourite of William III, he was a soldier and courtier made governor of Virginia in 1737 on Walpole's recommendation.
records.role_summary: No documented direct involvement in slavery; he drew the governor's salary for 17 years without ever going to America. The family's sharper link is through his sons: Augustus Keppel took the French slave-trading island of Gorée in 1758, and George Keppel, 3rd Earl, captured Havana in 1762, after which British traders sold enslaved Africans into Cuba during the 11-month occupation.

roleDetail.d: Encyclopedia Virginia: 'Albemarle never went to America'; Gooch and Dinwiddie governed in his name.
Augustus Keppel commanded the 1758 capture of Gorée; the 3rd Earl's 1762 Havana occupation opened the port to British slave sales (scale debated by historians).

records.legacy: Albemarle County (1744), home of Monticello and the University of Virginia, takes his title. The earldom continues in the Keppel family.

legacyDetail.d: Queen Camilla is a great-great-granddaughter of the 7th Earl of Albemarle through Alice and George Keppel.

records.name: Jeffery Amherst, 1st Baron Amherst
records.scaleNote: Absentee governor of Virginia 1759–68 (never visited); no documented slaveholding or slave-trade role found.
records.origins: A Kentish soldier who captured Louisbourg (1758) and Montreal (1760), he was rewarded with the governorship of Virginia, which he held without visiting.
records.role_summary: No documented direct involvement in slavery; his name matters because of his documented hostility to Native Americans: in 1763 he endorsed spreading smallpox among besieging Native people during Pontiac's War, and his refusal to provision Indian allies helped provoke that war.

roleDetail.d: Encyclopedia Virginia: governor from 1759, he never visited the colony; Fauquier governed in his name.
His 1763 letters with Henry Bouquet discussed infecting Native people with smallpox.

records.legacy: Amherst County (1761) and Amherst, Massachusetts, are named for him; Amherst College dropped its unofficial 'Lord Jeff' mascot in 2016 over his record toward Native Americans.

legacyDetail.d: Amherst College retired 'Lord Jeff' in 2016.

lineage.note: Inherited the barony; later Governor-General of India; the earldom became extinct in 1993.

records.today: The Amherst peerages became extinct in 1993. He had no children. No publicly documented descendants have addressed the link.

records.name: George Montagu-Dunk, 2nd Earl of Halifax

records.name: Virginia partus law of 1662 ('Negro womens children to serve according to the condition of the mother')
records.description: Passed in December 1662, it reversed English common law by making a child's status follow the mother (partus sequitur ventrem), so children of enslaved women were enslaved for life whoever the father was. It closed the route Elizabeth Key had used in 1656 to win freedom through her English father, and made slavery self-reproducing; the same act doubled fines for sex between Christians and Black people.

records.name: Virginia act declaring that baptism does not exempt from bondage (1667)
records.description: In September 1667 the General Assembly declared that baptism did not change an enslaved person's status, removing Christian conversion as a route to freedom and encouraging enslavers to baptise without fear of losing property. The rule was repeated in the 1705 code.

records.name: Virginia 'act about the casuall killing of slaves' (1669)
records.description: This 1669 act declared that a master who killed an enslaved person while 'correcting' them was not guilty of a felony, since no one would destroy his own estate with malice. It gave enslavers near-absolute power over life, and was carried into the 1705 code.

records.name: Virginia 'act for suppressing outlying slaves' (1691)
records.description: Passed 3 April 1691, it authorised sheriffs and posses to kill enslaved people 'lying out' who resisted capture (owners compensated 4,000 lb of tobacco), banned marriage between white and Black or Indian people, and required anyone freeing an enslaved person to pay to transport them out of Virginia within six months.

records.name: Virginia Slave Code of 1705 ('An act concerning Servants and Slaves')
records.description: Passed in October 1705, the 41-section act consolidated earlier laws into a comprehensive racial slave code: non-Christian imported servants became slaves, enslaved people were made real estate for inheritance, masters were immune for killing during correction, and enslaved people could be dismembered for running away. It became a model for other colonies.

records.name: Virginia 1723 act 'for the better government of Negros, Mulattos, and Indians, bond or free'
records.description: Passed in May 1723 under Lt Gov Hugh Drysdale after rumours of a conspiracy, it barred freeing any enslaved person except for 'meritorious services' approved by the governor and council, stripped free Black, mixed-race and Indian men of the vote, and tightened trials of enslaved people. Gov. Gooch defended the disfranchisement to the Board of Trade in 1735/36; the manumission ban lasted until 1782.

connections.label: Board of Trade review of colonial acts

records.name: Greenway Court (Lord Fairfax's manor and land office)
records.description: Thomas, 6th Lord Fairfax's estate near White Post in today's Clarke County, built c.1752, from which he ran the Northern Neck Proprietary's land office. Enslaved people lived in log quarters on the estate (NPS survey); Fairfax died there in 1781. The stone land office survives; the main house was replaced in 1828.

records.name: Germanna and Spotswood's ironworks
records.description: Frontier settlement founded c.1714 by Lt Gov Alexander Spotswood, who brought German miners and built the South's first ironworks, run with enslaved labour; Spotswood's mansion there (the 'enchanted castle') was abandoned by c.1750 and is an archaeological site.

events.title: James I charters the Virginia Company
events.text: The charter created the company that founded Jamestown in 1607; Virginia became a royal colony in 1624.

source.label: Encyclopedia Virginia — Virginia Company of London

events.title: First recorded Africans land in Virginia
events.text: About twenty captive Africans from a Portuguese slaver were landed at Point Comfort during James I's reign.

source.label: Encyclopedia Virginia — Colonial Virginia

events.title: Virginia makes slavery hereditary through the mother
events.text: Under Gov. Berkeley the assembly enacted that children follow the condition of the mother.

source.label: Encyclopedia Virginia — 1662 act

events.title: 'Casual killing' act
events.text: Masters who killed enslaved people during 'correction' were declared not guilty of felony.

source.label: Encyclopedia Virginia — 1669 act

events.title: Arlington subscribes to the new Royal African Company
events.text: Henry Bennet, Earl of Arlington, is listed among members in the RAC's 1672 charter.

source.label: Wikipedia — RAC officials and shareholders 1672

events.title: Colston transfers RAC stock to William III
events.text: Edward Colston transferred £1,000 of Royal African Company stock to the new king, a document published in 2023.

source.label: CBS News — King Charles supports research into monarchy's slavery links (2023)

events.title: Freed people must leave Virginia
events.text: The 'act for suppressing outlying slaves' required manumitted people to be transported out of the colony within six months.

source.label: Encyclopedia Virginia — 1691 act

events.title: William III assents to opening the slave trade
events.text: The Trade with Africa Act ended the RAC monopoly, letting separate traders ship captives on a 10% duty.

source.label: Wikipedia — Trade with Africa Act 1697

events.title: Virginia Slave Code
events.text: The assembly consolidated its slave laws into the 41-section 'act concerning Servants and Slaves'.

source.label: Encyclopedia Virginia — 1705 act

events.title: Britain wins the asiento
events.text: Queen Anne announced the asiento gained at Utrecht; it was assigned to the South Sea Company.

source.label: UMD Slavery, Law & Power — Queen Anne's speech

events.title: Manumission banned and free Black men disfranchised
events.text: Under Drysdale the assembly restricted manumission and removed free Black men's vote; Gooch later defended it.

source.label: Encyclopedia Virginia — Denying Free Blacks the Right to Vote

events.title: Britain seizes Senegal and Gorée
events.text: Pitt's ministry captured French Saint-Louis and, under Augustus Keppel, Gorée.

source.label: Wikipedia — British capture of Senegal

events.title: Dunmore's Proclamation
events.text: Gov. Dunmore offered freedom to enslaved people of rebels who fought for the King, while keeping his own enslaved workers.

source.label: Encyclopedia Virginia — Dunmore

events.title: Gov. Wise refuses to spare John Brown
events.text: Henry A. Wise declined to commute Brown's sentence; Brown was hanged on 2 December 1859.

source.label: Encyclopedia Virginia — Henry A. Wise

events.title: Lord Fairfax Community College drops his name
events.text: The board voted to rename the college because Fairfax was an enslaver; it became Laurel Ridge Community College.

source.label: InsideNoVa — Lord Fairfax Community College to change name
